In this notebook you will compare occupational injury statistics across countries, using
data that national governments report to the International Labour Organization (ILO).
Read the module [README](../README.md) and [data dictionary](../data_dictionary.md) first.

**How to use this notebook**

- Run each code chunk in order (the green arrow in RStudio, or Ctrl/Cmd + Shift + Enter).
- Answer the questions under each **Your answer** heading.
- When you are done, click **Knit** to produce an HTML report to submit.

# Part 0. Load the data

The three tables in `data/tidy/` are complete (not samples) and are committed to the
repository. To refresh them with the latest ILO data, run `scripts/fetch_data.R` and then
`scripts/build_dataset.R`.

```{r setup, message = FALSE}
library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(stringr)
library(forcats)
library(tidyr)

tidy_dir <- "../data/tidy"
github <- paste0("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/eddiekasner/occupational-safety-health-datasets/",
                 "main/modules/intl-ilostat-osh/data/tidy")

read_tidy <- function(name) {
  local <- file.path(tidy_dir, name)
  read_csv(if (file.exists(local)) local else file.path(github, name),
           col_types = cols(year = col_integer(), value = col_double(), .default = col_character()))
}

national <- read_tidy("injuries_national.csv")
by_sector <- read_tidy("injuries_by_sector.csv")
inspection <- read_tidy("labour_inspection.csv")
```

# Part 1. Get oriented

The tables are in **long** format: one row per country, year, breakdown and `measure`.

```{r orient}
glimpse(national)
count(national, measure)

# National totals: both sexes, all workers
totals <- national |> filter(sex == "Total", migrant_status == "Total")

latest_fatal <- totals |>
  filter(measure == "fatal_rate_per_100k", !is.na(value)) |>
  group_by(country_code) |>
  slice_max(year, n = 1) |>
  ungroup()

cat(n_distinct(latest_fatal$country_code), "countries have ever reported a fatal injury rate\n")

ggplot(latest_fatal, aes(year)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 2) +
  labs(title = "Most recent year with a fatal injury rate, by country", x = "Year", y = "Countries")
```

**Questions**

1. How many countries have reported a fatal injury rate since 2018? (Hint: `filter(latest_fatal, year >= 2018)`.)
2. Some of the world's largest economies have no recent data, or none at all. Search for
   China (`CHN`) and India (`IND`). What does this mean for any "global" comparison?
3. Who collects these numbers? (Look at the `source` column for five countries.)

# Part 2. Comparing fatal injury rates

```{r fatal-compare, fig.height = 9}
recent <- latest_fatal |> filter(year >= 2018)

ggplot(recent, aes(value, fct_reorder(country, value), colour = region)) +
  geom_point() +
  scale_x_log10() +
  labs(title = "Fatal occupational injuries per 100,000 workers (latest year since 2018)",
       x = "Rate (log scale)", y = NULL, colour = "Region")

recent |>
  arrange(desc(value)) |>
  select(country, year, value, source_type, source, notes) |>
  head(5)
```

**Questions**

1. Which country has by far the highest rate? Read its `source` and `notes`. Is this rate
   plausible? What would you check before reporting it? (Hint: what types of cases does it include?)
2. Compare two countries you know something about. What could explain the difference besides
   how dangerous work actually is?

**Your answer:**



# Part 3. Can we compare countries at all?

Countries collect injury data in different ways. The `notes` column records important
differences, such as whether the data cover **reported** or only **compensated** injuries,
and whether they include **commuting accidents** or **occupational diseases**.

```{r comparability}
recent |>
  mutate(coverage = str_extract(notes, "Coverage of occupational injuries: [^|]+"),
         case_types = str_extract(notes, "Type of cases of occupational injuries: [^|]+")) |>
  count(source_type, coverage, case_types, sort = TRUE)
```

A useful check is the ratio of **non-fatal** to **fatal** injuries. Fatal injuries are hard
to hide; non-fatal injuries are easy to leave unreported. Countries with good reporting
usually record hundreds or thousands of non-fatal injuries for every death.

```{r ratio, fig.height = 8}
ratio <- totals |>
  filter(measure %in% c("fatal_rate_per_100k", "nonfatal_rate_per_100k"), year >= 2015) |>
  select(country, region, year, measure, value) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = measure, values_from = value) |>
  filter(fatal_rate_per_100k > 0, !is.na(nonfatal_rate_per_100k)) |>
  group_by(country) |>
  slice_max(year, n = 1) |>
  ungroup() |>
  mutate(nonfatal_per_fatal = nonfatal_rate_per_100k / fatal_rate_per_100k)

ggplot(ratio, aes(nonfatal_per_fatal, fct_reorder(country, nonfatal_per_fatal), colour = region)) +
  geom_point() +
  scale_x_log10() +
  labs(title = "Non-fatal injuries reported for each fatal injury (latest year since 2015)",
       x = "Ratio (log scale)", y = NULL, colour = "Region")
```

**Questions**

1. Which countries report fewer than 10 non-fatal injuries per death? What does that suggest?
2. If you were asked to rank countries by workplace safety, would you use fatal rates,
   non-fatal rates, or neither? Explain.

**Your answer:**



# Part 4. Trends over time

```{r trends}
selected <- c("USA", "KOR", "MEX", "DEU", "AUS", "ESP")

totals |>
  filter(measure == "fatal_rate_per_100k", country_code %in% selected, year >= 1990) |>
  ggplot(aes(year, value, colour = source_type)) +
  geom_line(aes(group = 1)) +
  geom_point(size = 0.8) +
  facet_wrap(~ country, scales = "free_y") +
  labs(title = "Fatal occupational injury rates", x = NULL,
       y = "Per 100,000 workers", colour = "Source type")
```

**Questions**

1. Which countries show a clear decline? Which do not?
2. Look for changes in `source_type` or sudden jumps. Why is a change in the data source a

3. Pick one country and edit `selected` to add it. What happened there?

# Part 5. Which sectors are most dangerous?

```{r sectors, fig.height = 7}
sector_recent <- by_sector |>
  filter(measure == "fatal_rate_per_100k", classification == "ISIC Rev. 4",
         sector_code != "TOTAL", region == "Europe", year >= 2018) |>
  group_by(country, sector) |>
  slice_max(year, n = 1) |>
  ungroup()

sector_recent |>
  group_by(sector) |>
  summarise(countries = n(), median_rate = median(value, na.rm = TRUE)) |>
  filter(countries >= 10) |>
  arrange(desc(median_rate))

sector_recent |>
  filter(str_detect(sector, "^(A|B|C|F|H|Q)\\.")) |>
  ggplot(aes(value, fct_reorder(sector, value, .fun = median))) +
  geom_boxplot(outlier.shape = NA) +
  geom_jitter(height = 0.15, alpha = 0.5) +
  labs(title = "Fatal injury rates in European countries by sector (latest year since 2018)",
       x = "Per 100,000 workers", y = NULL)
```

**Questions**

1. Which sectors have the highest median fatal injury rates in Europe? Does this match what
   you know about the US (for example, from BLS's Census of Fatal Occupational Injuries)?
2. Why do we use the median across countries instead of the mean?
3. How might road traffic deaths during work, or deaths of self-employed farmers, be counted
   differently between countries? How would that affect sectors A and H?

**Your answer:**



# Part 6. Migrant workers

```{r migrants}
migrant <- national |>
  filter(measure == "fatal_rate_per_100k", sex == "Total",
         migrant_status %in% c("Migrants", "Non migrants"), !is.na(value)) |>
  select(country, year, migrant_status, value) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = migrant_status, values_from = value) |>
  filter(!is.na(Migrants), !is.na(`Non migrants`)) |>
  group_by(country) |>
  slice_max(year, n = 1) |>
  ungroup() |>
  mutate(ratio = Migrants / `Non migrants`)

arrange(migrant, desc(ratio))
```

**Questions**

1. In how many countries is the fatal rate higher for migrant workers? Lower?
2. Migrant workers are often concentrated in dangerous jobs, but they may also be less likely
   to appear in the records (undocumented work, no insurance) and in the denominator.
   How could each of these bias the ratio?

**Your answer:**



# Part 7. Labour inspection and fatal injuries

The ILO's commonly cited benchmark is about **one labour inspector per 10,000 workers** in
industrial market economies (fewer in developing economies).

```{r inspection}
inspectors <- inspection |>
  filter(measure == "inspectors_per_10k_employed", !is.na(value)) |>
  group_by(country_code) |>
  slice_max(year, n = 1) |>
  ungroup() |>
  select(country_code, country, region, inspectors_per_10k = value, inspection_year = year)

combined <- inspectors |>
  inner_join(select(latest_fatal, country_code, fatal_rate = value, fatal_year = year),
             by = "country_code") |>
  filter(abs(inspection_year - fatal_year) <= 3, fatal_rate > 0)

ggplot(combined, aes(inspectors_per_10k, fatal_rate, colour = region)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 1, linetype = "dashed") +
  scale_x_log10() +
  scale_y_log10() +
  labs(title = "Labour inspectors and fatal injury rates",
       x = "Inspectors per 10,000 employed (log scale)",
       y = "Fatal injuries per 100,000 workers (log scale)", colour = "Region")

cor.test(combined$inspectors_per_10k, combined$fatal_rate, method = "spearman", exact = FALSE)
```

**Questions**

1. Describe the relationship. Is it what you expected?
2. Give one reason why more inspectors could lead to **lower** fatal rates, and one reason why
   more inspectors could lead to **higher** reported rates.
3. Check the arithmetic: for one country, compute `fatal_cases / (workers_covered_thousands * 1000) * 100000`
   from the `national` table and compare it with `fatal_rate_per_100k`. Do they match?

**Your answer:**
